why.note: Since 1971 the dollar has lost about 80% of its value against the franc. Yet the franc is around 1% of world payments and only 0.015% of stablecoins. The Swiss Bankers Association puts the potential for CHF stablecoins at CHF 2.8–3.0bn at today's market size.

membership.title: What the Association does
membership.subtitle: The Frankencoin Association promotes a stable Swiss franc and a digital Swiss economy, at home and globally. Membership is by invitation.
membership.role: The Association is not the issuer of ZCHF and does not control the Frankencoin protocol. ZCHF is created by users who lock collateral in autonomous smart contracts on Ethereum. Changes to the protocol are decided by the holders of Frankencoin Shares (FCS) through on-chain governance, open to anyone. The Association holds no custody of user funds.
membership.roleMore: Under MiCA, ZCHF is a crypto-asset with no identifiable issuer. The Association has published a MiCA-format white paper for ZCHF, which is listed in ESMA's interim MiCA register.

roleLink.label: Legal opinions, MiCA white paper and register entry

membership.title: Was der Verein tut
membership.subtitle: Der Frankencoin-Verein fördert einen stabilen Schweizer Franken und eine digitale Schweizer Wirtschaft, im Inland und weltweit. Die Mitgliedschaft erfolgt auf Einladung.
membership.role: Der Verein ist nicht der Emittent von ZCHF und kontrolliert das Frankencoin-Protokoll nicht. ZCHF wird von Nutzern geschaffen, die Sicherheiten in autonomen Smart Contracts auf Ethereum hinterlegen. Über Änderungen am Protokoll entscheiden die Inhaber von Frankencoin Shares (FCS) in der On-Chain-Governance, die allen offensteht. Der Verein verwahrt keine Kundengelder.
membership.roleMore: Unter MiCA ist ZCHF ein Krypto-Asset ohne identifizierbaren Emittenten. Der Verein hat ein White Paper im MiCA-Format für ZCHF veröffentlicht, das im vorläufigen MiCA-Register der ESMA geführt wird.

src/content/en/compliance.json.heroTitle: Classified in Switzerland.|Documented for the EU.
src/content/en/compliance.json.intro: Two independent legal assessments by LEXR describe how ZCHF and the pool shares fit Swiss and EU law. This page summarises them; the documents themselves are linked below.

rows.title: Switzerland
rows.body: According to the assessment by LEXR Law Switzerland AG (August 2024), ZCHF qualifies as a payment token and a currency-linked stablecoin under FINMA's guidelines, not as a security, and using it to pay for goods and services is generally outside Swiss financial market law. The same assessment classifies the pool shares (FPS) as a utility token that gives access to governance.

rows.title: European Union
rows.body: According to the opinion by LEXR Germany Rechtsanwalts GmbH (February 2026), ZCHF is a crypto-asset under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) with no identifiable issuer, so the issuer duties of MiCA Titles II to IV do not apply to it. A MiCA-format white paper for ZCHF has been published and appears in ESMA's interim MiCA register. The register entry records the white paper; it is not an approval or endorsement by ESMA or any authority. Terms: asset-referenced tokens (ART) and electronic money tokens (EMT).

cta.label: EU MiCA legal opinion (PDF)
cta.href: /20260209 ZCHF MiCA Frankencoin Association Public Summary FINAL.pdf

rows.title: Service providers
rows.body: Exchanges, custodians and other crypto-asset service providers that handle ZCHF remain subject to their own licensing, anti-money-laundering and consumer-protection obligations in their jurisdiction. The assessments describe the token, not the obligations of the businesses that offer it.

boiler.title: About Frankencoin
boiler.text: Frankencoin (ZCHF) is a decentralized stablecoin that tracks the Swiss franc. It is issued by smart contracts against on-chain collateral rather than by a company, has been live since 2023 and is available on eight blockchains. Frankencoin Shares (FCS) represent the protocol's equity. The Frankencoin Association in Switzerland supports its development.
boiler.note: Reuse as is or shorten; please do not describe ZCHF as bank-issued or as backed by bank deposits.

src/content/en/use-cases.json.title: Where ZCHF is used today
src/content/en/use-cases.json.intro: Services that take, hold or pay out Frankencoin, grouped by what you want to do. Each card says the concrete route.

cases.title: Buy and sell ZCHF
cases.description: Buy, sell and trade ZCHF on Kraken, with the option to withdraw to your own wallet.

cases.title: Swiss IBAN and card payments
cases.description: Fund your personal Swiss IBAN to receive ZCHF in ether.fi, spend it with the card or use it as borrowing collateral. Send CHF back to a Swiss bank account in your own name.

cases.title: Pay at the till
cases.description: Pay at the checkout of over 100 Spar stores in Switzerland: the cashier shows a QR code, you confirm from a wallet that holds ZCHF.

cases.title: Online checkout
cases.description: Merchants add a crypto checkout to Shopify, WooCommerce, BigCommerce or a custom shop. Customers pay in ZCHF; the merchant withdraws to a wallet they control.

cases.title: Buy with a bank transfer, pay bills
cases.description: Buy ZCHF by bank transfer to your own wallet, or link the wallet to a personal IBAN to receive transfers and pay Swiss QR bills in ZCHF.

cases.title: Visa card
cases.description: Zeal is the wallet app, Gnosis Pay issues the Visa debit card. Hold ZCHF in Zeal and spend it anywhere Visa is accepted; the card settles from your ZCHF balance.

cases.title: Protocol savings
cases.description: Deposit ZCHF in the protocol's savings module to earn the rate set by governance. Interest starts after an initial waiting period; you can withdraw at any time.

cases.title: Recurring savings plan
cases.description: Set up a recurring savings plan in ZCHF or BTC, for yourself or for someone else. Funds stay in your own wallet and the ZCHF part earns the protocol savings rate.

cases.title: Savings app with IBAN
cases.description: Fund a personal IBAN by bank transfer or deposit digital assets, allocate to a ZCHF, EUR or USD strategy, and withdraw when you need the money.

cases.title: Lend or borrow ZCHF
cases.description: Supply ZCHF to earn interest from borrowers, or borrow ZCHF against crypto collateral, in Morpho's lending markets on Ethereum and Base.

cases.title: Borrow crvUSD against svZCHF
cases.description: Deposit savings-vault tokens (svZCHF) as collateral and borrow crvUSD in Curve's isolated Ethereum market. Rates and liquidation terms are set by that market.

cases.title: Index fund component
cases.description: ZCHF is one of the components of the ixEDEL index fund on Reserve Protocol, alongside gold, Bitcoin and yield-bearing stablecoins.

cases.title: Tokenized shares
cases.description: Buy and sell tokenized shares of Swiss companies, and take part in their capital raises, with ZCHF as the settlement currency.

cases.title: Payroll
cases.description: Run payroll, social insurance and pension contributions for employees and settle the wages in ZCHF.

cases.title: Company treasury and rental deposits
cases.description: Treasury products for companies built on ZCHF, including rental deposits held in ZCHF.

cases.title: Custody
cases.description: Hold ZCHF in custody with Bitcoin Suisse, a Swiss crypto financial services provider, instead of in your own wallet.

cases.title: Institutional custody
cases.description: Institutions hold ZCHF in Copper's custody and can deploy it to DeFi from there, next to the rest of their digital assets.

questions.question: What is Frankencoin?
questions.answer: Frankencoin (ZCHF) is a decentralized stablecoin that tracks the Swiss franc. It is not issued by a company: anyone can mint it against collateral worth more than the ZCHF they create, and the collateral stays visible on-chain. See [What is Frankencoin](/what-is-frankencoin).

questions.question: What is a stablecoin?
questions.answer: A digital token designed to hold a stable value against a reference currency. For ZCHF the reference is the Swiss franc; each ZCHF is backed by collateral worth more than one franc.

questions.question: How is Frankencoin different from a bank account in CHF?
questions.answer: A bank balance is a claim on one bank. ZCHF is a token you hold in your own wallet, backed by collateral anyone can inspect on-chain, and no institution can freeze it. It is not a deposit and is not covered by deposit insurance.

questions.question: How is Frankencoin different from USDT or USDC?
questions.answer: USDT and USDC are issued by companies against reserves they hold, and the issuer can freeze balances. ZCHF is issued by smart contracts against on-chain collateral, tracks the franc rather than the dollar, and has no issuer who can freeze it. See the [comparison](/compare).

questions.question: Is Frankencoin backed 1:1 by Swiss francs?
questions.answer: No. The franc is the reference currency, not the backing. Each ZCHF is backed by collateral (BTC, ETH, tokenized gold or shares) worth more than one franc. See [How it works](/how-it-works).

questions.question: What does 'over-collateralized' mean?
questions.answer: The collateral is worth more than the ZCHF minted against it. To mint 100 ZCHF, a borrower might lock ETH worth 150 francs. The extra 50 francs is the buffer that absorbs price drops before the system is at risk.

questions.question: What happens if the collateral loses value?
questions.answer: Each position has a liquidation price. If the collateral falls below it, anyone can challenge the position and its collateral is sold at [auction](https://docs.frankencoin.com/positions/auctions) to repay the debt. If an auction does not cover the debt, the shortfall is taken from the protocol [reserve](https://docs.frankencoin.com/reserve).

questions.question: How do FCS and FPS differ?
questions.answer: FCS (Frankencoin Shares) is the share and governance token: a claim on the reserve plus a vote. FPS (Frankencoin Pool Shares) is the earlier equity token that FCS wraps one-to-one; existing FPS can be wrapped into FCS. See [FCS](/fcs).

questions.question: Can Frankencoin lose its peg to the Swiss franc?
questions.answer: ZCHF can trade slightly above or below one franc. Because borrowers owe exactly one franc of debt per ZCHF, deviations are arbitrage opportunities that pull the price back. There is no issuer who redeems at one franc on demand.

questions.question: Where can I use Frankencoin?
questions.answer: In Spar stores in Switzerland, via Gnosis Pay and Zeal for card payments, with Mt Pelerin for bank transfers, in payroll with Quitt and in DeFi on Morpho and Curve. See all [use cases](/use-cases).

questions.question: How do I get Frankencoin?
questions.answer: Buy it on an exchange or DEX, convert francs through Mt Pelerin or DFX, or mint it yourself against collateral in the [app](https://app.frankencoin.com/mint). See [exchanges and wallets](/for/exchanges-wallets).

questions.question: Can I earn interest on my Frankencoin?
questions.answer: Yes, by depositing ZCHF in the [savings module](https://app.frankencoin.com/savings), which pays the protocol rate set by governance. Holding ZCHF in a wallet does not earn anything by itself. The rate can change and is not guaranteed. See [Save in CHF](/use-cases/save-in-chf).

questions.question: Is Frankencoin regulated?
questions.answer: Legal assessments obtained by the Frankencoin Association classify ZCHF as a payment token under Swiss law and as a crypto-asset under MiCA, with some provisions not applying to a protocol without an issuer. The protocol itself is not licensed or supervised. See [Compliance](/compliance).

questions.question: What are the risks?
questions.answer: Smart contract bugs, a sharp fall in collateral prices that liquidations cannot cover, ZCHF trading away from one franc, and thin liquidity when you want to sell. The contracts are [audited](/security), but no system is risk-free.

questions.question: What is the Frankencoin Association?
questions.answer: A Swiss non-profit based in Zug that supports development and the ecosystem and serves as a [point of contact](mailto:hello@frankencoin.com). It does not control the protocol.

questions.question: Has Frankencoin been audited?
questions.answer: Yes, by Code4rena, Blockbite and ChainSecurity. The reports are on the [Security](/security) page.
